summary: Lecture 6 of MIT 6.254 (Game Theory with Engineering Applications, Asu Ozdaglar, Feb 23 2010) covers continuous games and discontinuous games. It proves Glicksberg's theorem that every continuous game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium by approximating the game with essentially finite games, applying Nash's theorem, and taking limits under the weak topology. It then gives discontinuous-game examples (Bertrand competition with capacity constraints, Hotelling competition) and gives conditions for uniqueness of pure strategy Nash equilibrium via diagonal strict concavity (Rosen's framework, KKT conditions, Proposition 4 on negative definite symmetric Jacobian).
one_line: MIT lecture on continuous and discontinuous games, covering Glicksberg's existence theorem, Bertrand and Hotelling examples, and conditions for unique pure Nash equilibrium.
key_facts: Glicksberg's Theorem states that every continuous game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium.
A continuous game is defined with a finite player set I, nonempty compact metric strategy spaces Si, and continuous utility functions ui.
An epsilon-equilibrium is a mixed strategy σ such that ui(si, σ−i) ≤ ui(σi, σ−i) + ε for all players i and strategies si in Si.
Proposition 2 states that if G' is an α-approximation to G and σ is an ε-equilibrium of G', then σ is an (ε + 2α)-equilibrium of G.
Proposition 3 states that for any continuous game G and any α > 0, there exists an essentially finite game that is an α-approximation to G.
The proof of Glicksberg's Theorem uses a scalar sequence αk decreasing to 0, Nash's Theorem for each essentially finite approximation, and compactness of Σ to extract a convergent subsequence.
In the Bertrand example with capacity constraints of 2/3 each, there is no pure strategy Nash equilibrium because either firm can raise its price and still sell 1/3 units.
In the capacity-constrained Bertrand example, the symmetric mixed strategy CDF is F(p) = 0 for 0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2, F(p) = 2 − 1/p for 1/2 ≤ p ≤ 1, and F(p) = 1 for p ≥ 1.
In the Hotelling example with n = 3 candidates, the lecture shows there is no pure strategy Nash equilibrium and asks for a mixed strategy equilibrium.
Example 3 has payoffs u1 = s1s2 − s1²/2 and u2 = s1s2 − s2²/2 on [0,1] for both players, and every profile (x, x) with x in [0,1] is a pure strategy Nash equilibrium.

Theorem 4 states that if strategy sets are given by concave constraints hi(xi) ≥ 0 with a strictly feasible point, and payoffs are diagonally strictly concave, then the game has a unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium.
Diagonally strictly concave means that for all x*, x̄ in S, (x̄ − x*)^T ∇u(x*) + (x* − x̄)^T ∇u(x̄) > 0.
Proposition 4 states that if the symmetric matrix U(x) + U^T(x) is negative definite for all x in S, then the payoff functions are diagonally strictly concave.
The lecture credits the uniqueness result to Rosen's 1965 Econometrica paper on existence and uniqueness of equilibrium points for concave N-person games.
Myerson's Game Theory: Analysis of Conflict (1991), pp. 140-148, is the lecture's main source for the development of continuous games.
